title: Your rights at a protest
disclaimer: General legal information, not legal advice.

items.point: Every citizen has a right to speak out and to gather with others peacefully and without weapons.
items.quote: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms;
items.note: Text from the Legislative Department's Constitution 'As on 1st May, 2026'. These rights belong to citizens.

items.point: The government can put reasonable limits on gatherings by law, for public order or the sovereignty and integrity of India, but only reasonable ones.
items.quote: (3) Nothing in sub-clause (b) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause.
items.note: Article 19(2) lists more grounds for speech (security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence).

items.topic: 1. Peaceful protest is a basic feature of democracy
items.point: The Supreme Court has said that peaceful protest is part of democracy and the government should respect it.
items.law: In re Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary, Supreme Court, 23 February 2012, para 200 (Swatanter Kumar J.)
items.quote: Freedom of speech, right to assemble and demonstrate by holding dharnas and peaceful agitations are the basic features of a democratic system. The people of a democratic country like ours have a right to raise their voice against the decisions and actions of the Government
items.note: Reported as (2012) 5 SCC 1; that citation was not shown on the page opened, so the owner should confirm it. Do not use the line 'Citizens have a fundamental right to assembly and peaceful protest which cannot be taken away by an arbitrary executive or legislative action': in this judgment it is a party's submission (para 81), not the Court's finding.

items.topic: 2. Prohibitory orders: who and how long
items.point: A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or a specially empowered Executive Magistrate can issue a written order banning certain acts in an area. It lasts at most two months, unless the State Government extends it by up to six months more.
items.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 163(1), (3), (4) (replaces CrPC section 144)
items.quote: No order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from the making thereof: Provided that if the State Government considers it necessary so to do for preventing danger to human life, health or safety or for preventing a riot or any affray, it may, by notification, direct that an order made by a Magistrate under this section shall remain in force for such further period not exceeding six months
items.note: Section 163(1) also requires 'a written order stating the material facts of the case'; 163(3) lets it apply 'to the public generally when frequenting or visiting a particular place or area'.

items.topic: 2. Prohibitory orders: you can ask for one to be cancelled
items.point: Anyone affected can ask the Magistrate (or the State Government, for an extension) to cancel or change the order, and must be given a chance to be heard.
items.quote: Any Magistrate may, either on his own motion or on the application of any person aggrieved, rescind or alter any order made under this section
items.note: 163(7): the applicant gets 'an early opportunity of appearing before him or it, either in person or by an advocate', and a rejection must be reasoned in writing.

items.point: Knowingly disobeying a lawful prohibitory order is itself an offence.
items.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 223 (replaces IPC section 188)
items.quote: Whoever, knowing that, by an order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order, he is directed to abstain from a certain act, ... disobeys such direction,–– (a) shall, if such disobedience causes or tends to cause obstruction, annoyance or injury, ... be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both;
items.note: Clause (b) of s.223 (higher punishment where disobedience endangers life, health or safety or causes a riot) was not extracted; read the gazette page before quoting it.

items.topic: 2. Supreme Court tests for prohibitory orders
items.point: The Supreme Court has said these orders are for emergencies, cannot be used to suppress legitimate protest, must state the facts behind them, must use the least restrictive measure, and cannot be repeated again and again.
items.law: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 10 January 2020, para 140 (AIR 2020 SC 1308; (2020) 3 SCC 637)
items.quote: ii. The power under Section 144, Cr.P.C cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression of opinion or grievance or exercise of any democratic rights. iii. An order passed under Section 144, Cr.P.C. should state the material facts to enable judicial review of the same. ... iv. While exercising the power under Section 144, Cr.P.C. the Magistrate is duty bound to balance the rights and restrictions based on the principles of proportionality and thereafter apply the least intrusive measure. v. Repetitive orders under Section 144, Cr.P.C. would be an abuse of power.
items.note: Decided under CrPC s.144. BNSS s.163 reproduces its substance, so the tests should carry over, but no judgment applying them to s.163 by name was checked. The SCC citation is from memory; the page shows AIR 2020 SC 1308.

items.point: The Court has also said such orders apply only in emergencies, though authorities may control the time and place of a meeting.
items.law: In re Ramlila Maidan Incident, Supreme Court, 23 February 2012
items.quote: However, it must be borne in mind that the provisions of Section 144 Cr.P.C. are attracted only in emergent situations. The emergent power is to be exercised for the purposes of maintaining public order.

items.point: A gathering of five or more people becomes an 'unlawful assembly' only if their shared aim is something like using criminal force against the government or officials, resisting the law, committing an offence, or forcing people by criminal force. A gathering that starts lawful can become unlawful later.
items.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 189(1) and Explanation (replaces IPC section 141)
items.quote: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is— (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government ... (b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or (c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; ... Explanation.—An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.

items.topic: 3. Staying after an order to disperse
items.point: Knowingly joining or staying in an unlawful assembly is punishable; staying after it has been lawfully ordered to disperse carries a higher punishment. Staying in any gathering of five or more likely to disturb the peace after a lawful order to disperse is also an offence.
items.quote: (3) Whoever joins or continues in an unlawful assembly, knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
items.note: 189(2): up to six months for intentionally joining or continuing in an unlawful assembly. 189(5): up to six months for staying in an assembly 'likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace, after such assembly has been lawfully commanded to disperse'. Section 190 (liability of every member for offences committed in prosecution of the common object) also exists and was seen but not extracted.

items.topic: 3. Who can order a crowd to disperse
items.point: An Executive Magistrate, the officer in charge of the police station or, in his absence, a police officer of at least sub-inspector rank can order an unlawful assembly, or a gathering of five or more likely to disturb the peace, to disperse. Members then have a duty to leave; if they do not, force may be used.
items.quote: Any Executive Magistrate or officer in charge of a police station or, in the absence of such officer in charge, any police officer, not below the rank of a sub-inspector, may command any unlawful assembly, or any assembly of five or more persons likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace, to disperse; and it shall thereupon be the duty of the members of such assembly to disperse accordingly.
items.note: Section 149 allows dispersal by the armed forces on the order of the District Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate he authorises, if the assembly 'cannot otherwise be dispersed', using 'as little force, and do as little injury to person and property, as may be consistent' with dispersing it. Section 150 covers armed forces acting when no Magistrate can be reached.

items.topic: 4. Protest areas cannot simply be banned
items.point: The Supreme Court held that a blanket ban on protests at Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club in Delhi was not allowed; the police may regulate protests there with guidelines and permission, not ban them altogether.
items.law: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 23 July 2018, paras 69-70 (AIR 2018 SC 3476)
items.quote: However, in reality no such activities are allowed at all and, therefore, the situation which is created amounts to ‘banning’ these public meetings, demonstrations, dharnas, etc. altogether rather than ‘regulating’ the same. 70) In the aforesaid conspectus, here also the Commissioner of Police, New Delhi and other official respondents can frame proper guidelines for regulating such protests, demonstrations, etc.
items.note: Often cited as (2018) 17 SCC 324; that citation was not shown on the page opened. The page number marker 'Page 69 of 72' sits inside the quoted passage in the source and has been dropped.

items.topic: 4. Public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely
items.point: The Supreme Court held that protesters cannot block a public road or occupy a public space indefinitely, and that protests must be held at designated places.
items.law: Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police, Supreme Court, 7 October 2020 (AIR 2020 SC 4704)
items.quote: we have to make it unequivocally clear that public ways and public spaces cannot be occupied in such a manner and that too indefinitely. Democracy and dissent go hand in hand, but then the demonstrations expressing dissent have to be in designated places alone.
items.note: Usually cited as (2020) 10 SCC 439; not shown on the page opened.

items.point: Whether you need police permission, and where you may protest, is set by state police Acts and local orders, and differs from state to state and city to city. Check with the local police station or a lawyer before the day.
items.law: Example: the Delhi prohibitory order considered in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018)
items.quote: the orders prohibited these meetings etc. without written permission. In other words, before holding any such public meetings, processions, demonstrations, etc. prior permission of the authorities was required which should be considered on case to case basis.
items.note: This is the Delhi Police's own argument as recorded in the judgment (para 24), used only as an example of a permission requirement. No state police Act was opened, so none is named.

items.point: If arrested, you must be told the grounds of arrest as soon as possible, and you can consult and be defended by a lawyer of your choice.
items.quote: No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.
items.note: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons held under a preventive detention law from clauses (1) and (2).

items.point: You must be taken before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (not counting travel time), and cannot be held longer without the magistrate's order.
items.law: Constitution of India, Article 22(2); BNSS 2023, sections 57 and 58
items.quote: Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.
items.note: BNSS s.58: no detention without warrant beyond 'twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey' 'in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 187'.

items.topic: 5. Full particulars of the offence, and bail
items.point: Police arresting without a warrant must immediately tell you the full details of the offence. For a bailable offence they must tell you that you can be released on bail.
items.quote: (1) Every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest. (2) Where a police officer arrests without warrant any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence, he shall inform the person arrested that he is entitled to be released on bail and that he may arrange for sureties on his behalf.

items.topic: 5. Someone you name must be told
items.point: The police must at once tell a relative, friend or other person you name that you have been arrested and where you are being held, and tell you of this right at the police station.
items.quote: Every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his relatives, friends or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information and also to the designated police officer in the district.
items.note: 48(4): the Magistrate must check this was done.

items.point: The arresting officer must wear a clear name identification and prepare an arrest memo, witnessed by a family member or a respectable local person and signed by you.
items.law: BNSS 2023, section 36 (replaces CrPC section 41B); D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal, (1997) 1 SCC 416, decided 18 December 1996, requirements (1)-(2)
items.quote: Every police officer while making an arrest shall— (a) bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification; (b) prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be— (i) attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable member of the locality where the arrest is made; (ii) countersigned by the person arrested; and (c) inform the person arrested, unless the memorandum is attested by a member of his family, that he has a right to have a relative or a friend or any other person named by him to be informed of his arrest.
items.note: D.K. Basu (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/501198/) requirement (1): officers 'should bear accurate, visible and clear identification and name togs [sic, 'tags'] with their designations. The particulars of all such police personnel who handle interrogation of the arrestee must be recorded in a register.' Requirement (2) adds that the memo 'shall contain the time and date of arrest'. The 'togs' typo is in the Indian Kanoon text.

items.point: You may meet a lawyer of your choice during police questioning, though not for the whole of it.
items.law: BNSS 2023, section 38 (replaces CrPC section 41D); D.K. Basu requirement (10)
items.quote: When any person is arrested and interrogated by the police, he shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation.

items.topic: 5. Notice to appear instead of arrest
items.point: For offences punishable with up to seven years, police must issue a notice to appear instead of arresting you when arrest is not necessary. If you comply with the notice, you should not be arrested unless the officer records reasons.
items.quote: (3) The police officer shall, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1) issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence, to appear before him or at such other place as may be specified in the notice. ... (5) Where such person complies and continues to comply with the notice, he shall not be arrested in respect of the offence referred to in the notice unless, for reasons to be recorded, the police officer is of the opinion that he ought to be arrested.
items.note: 35(1)(b) requires reasons in writing for arresting, and its proviso requires reasons in writing for not arresting. 35(6): failing to comply, or being 'unwilling to identify himself', allows arrest. 35(7): no arrest without a DSP's permission for an offence punishable with less than three years where the person 'is infirm or is above sixty years of age'.

items.point: After arrest you must be examined by a government medical officer, or a registered medical practitioner if none is available, soon after the arrest.
items.quote: When any person is arrested, he shall be examined by a medical officer in the service of the Central Government or a State Government, and in case the medical officer is not available, by a registered medical practitioner soon after the arrest is made:
items.note: The proviso and later sub-sections of s.53 (e.g. examination of a woman by or under a female medical officer, and the copy of the report) were not extracted; read the gazette before stating them.

items.topic: 6. Women: no arrest at night, save exceptionally
items.point: A woman should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise. In exceptional cases a woman police officer must first get written permission from a first-class Magistrate.
items.quote: (5) Save in exceptional circumstances, no woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, and where such exceptional circumstances exist, the woman police officer shall, by making a written report, obtain the prior permission of the Magistrate of the first class within whose local jurisdiction the offence is committed or the arrest is to be made.

items.topic: 6. Women: not to be touched by a male officer
items.point: When a woman is arrested, her submission is presumed from being told orally, and a male officer should not touch her unless circumstances require it. Only a woman may search a woman.
items.quote: Provided that where a woman is to be arrested, unless the circumstances indicate to the contrary, her submission to custody on an oral intimation of arrest shall be presumed and, unless the circumstances otherwise require or unless the police officer is a female, the police officer shall not touch the person of the woman for making her arrest.
items.note: s.49(2): 'Whenever it is necessary to cause a female to be searched, the search shall be made by another female with strict regard to decency.' No BNSS provision was found requiring that a woman be arrested only by or with a woman officer 'where practicable'; the brief's wording should not be used. The nearest provisions are 43(1) proviso and 43(5).

items.point: The Constitution directs the State to provide free legal aid so that nobody is denied justice because they are poor or disadvantaged.
items.quote: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.
items.note: A Directive Principle; enforced in practice through the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

items.point: Anyone in custody is entitled to free legal services, as are all women and children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, industrial workers and people on low incomes.
items.law: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, section 12 (with section 13)
items.quote: Every person who has to file or defend a case shall be entitled to legal services under this Act if that person is — (a) a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; ... (c) a woman or a child; ... (g) in custody, ...
items.note: Copy from NALSA's own site. 12(h): income below Rs 9,000 a year, 'or such other higher amount as may be prescribed by the State Government' (Rs 12,000 or higher prescribed amount in the Supreme Court). States have raised these limits by notification and the limit differs by state; the current figures were not checked. 12(d) in NALSA's copy still refers to the 1995 Persons with Disabilities Act. s.13: the Authority must be satisfied there is a prima facie case, and an income affidavit is normally enough.

items.point: The national legal aid helpline number is 15100 (toll-free).
items.quote: 15100 NALSA Helpline Toll-Free Number
items.note: Read from the NALSA home page on 9 October 2026; its menu also lists 'NALSA Helpline Number 15100'.

omitted.reason: No judgment was found and opened that clearly states a right to photograph or record police in public. Omitted as instructed.
Not directly relevant to a citizen's protest about the SIR (the Code binds parties and candidates during an election). Omitted.

uncertain: BNSS and BNS text is the Gazette of India (Extraordinary) as enacted on 25 December 2023, hosted by the Ministry of Home Affairs. indiacode.nic.in timed out, so any amendment after enactment was not checked against an updated text.

BNSS s.1(2): apart from Chapters IX, XI and XII, the Sanhita does not apply to Nagaland and certain tribal areas unless extended. The arrest provisions (Chapter V) may not apply there. Chapter XI (ss.148-163) does apply.

Supreme Court judgments were read on indiankanoon.org (a judgments site), not on sci.gov.in. SCC citations for Ramlila (2012) 5 SCC 1, MKSS (2018) 17 SCC 324, Amit Sahni (2020) 10 SCC 439 and Anuradha Bhasin (2020) 3 SCC 637 were not displayed on the pages opened; the AIR citations were. D.K. Basu's 1997 (1) SCC 416 was displayed.
Anuradha Bhasin and Ramlila interpret CrPC s.144. BNSS s.163 reproduces its wording, but no judgment applying them to s.163 was checked.
Permission requirements under state police Acts and city police orders were not verified for any state; the page should say only that they vary and are set locally.
